study_identification_part.si4_title: Accommodating Site Variation In Neuroimaging Data Using Normative And Hierarchical Bayesian Models

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To develop and evaluate hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling approaches that accommodate site effects in multi-site neuroimaging data by modeling site as a random effect, and to compare their performance against common harmonization techniques such as ComBat and regressing out site effects.

rci11_site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The core contribution of this paper is modeling site as a random effect within the normative modeling framework rather than harmonizing data beforehand. The hierarchical Bayesian approach uses partial pooling where site-specific parameters originate from a shared first-order prior distribution. The paper compares this approach to several harmonization methods (ComBat, modified ComBat preserving age/sex, regressing out site) and demonstrates superior performance.
rci11_site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: For modeling site effects, introducing a hierarchical structure has the benefit that it allows to include structural dependencies between sites via partial pooling. Thus, instead of modeling site effects as an effect shared between sites or independently from each other, a semi-independent association between sites can be obtained via assuming that all site parameters originate from a shared first-order prior distribution... We hence induce shared priors and hyper priors θ 0 for site s... In contrast to other methods of harmonizing for additive and multiplicative site effects in the data prior to the normative modeling (e.g., regressing out site effects, harmonization with ComBat ), our approach is based on modeling site as predictor within the normative modeling framework in a single regression model.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Percentage of individuals with atypical z-scores (|z| ≥ 1.96) compared between autism and healthy control test sets; ANOVA with site as predictor to test residual site effects in z-scores (separate tests for training, test HC, and autism sets); comparison of regional distribution of atypical z-scores between clinical and control groups; visual inspection of spatial distribution of deviations across cortical regions
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Hierarchical Bayesian models (HBLM and HBGPM) that explicitly model site as random effects outperformed harmonization methods (ComBat, regressing out site) across all performance metrics, substantially reduced site effects in z-scores while retaining clinically useful variance, with autism samples showing higher rates of atypical deviations (7-8%) compared to controls (5-6%).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The hierarchical Bayesian models (HBLM and HBGPM) demonstrated superior performance compared to all comparison harmonization methods across multiple metrics: higher correlations between true and predicted values (ρ̄ ≈ 0.69-0.75 vs. 0.3-0.5 for comparison models), lower SRMSE (0.06-0.07 vs. 0.08-0.12), higher explained variance (EV = 0.48-0.57 vs. 0.07-0.33), better log-likelihood values (closer to zero), and negative MSLL in test sets (indicating better prediction than training mean). The non-linear HBGPM did not significantly outperform the linear HBLM, likely due to the restricted age range (6-40 years) where age-cortical thickness relationships are mostly linear. Harmonization methods suffered substantial variance shrinkage, retaining only 8-29% of original variance compared to 57-65% for hierarchical Bayesian models. Site effects were effectively reduced in z-scores: ANOVA showed site could not be predicted from z-scores in HBLM (p=1 for training set, p=0.063 for test set) compared to p<0.001 in uncorrected data. Application to autism samples demonstrated retention of clinically meaningful variance: 7.8% (HBGPM) and 7.2% (HBLM) of autism individuals showed atypical z-scores compared to the expected 5.7% and 5.5% in healthy controls, confirming both proper calibration and sensitivity to clinical differences. Partial η² for site effects was reduced from 0.55-0.58 in raw data to <0.001-0.17 after hierarchical Bayesian correction.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The paper demonstrates that normative z-scores can serve as 'cleaned' measures accounting for site, age, and sex effects for downstream analyses. The hierarchical Bayesian framework allows using posterior distributions from training sites as informed priors for new unseen sites (as demonstrated by Kia et al. 2020), though this was not implemented in the current study. The method avoids the variance removal problem inherent in two-stage harmonization approaches by integrating site effects within the normative modeling framework itself. Stan code is publicly available at https://github.com/likeajumprope/Bayesian_normative_models.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study is a replication and extension of Kia et al. (2020), adding a Gaussian Process version (HBGPM) to model non-linear age effects in addition to the linear hierarchical Bayesian model (HBLM). Data from 20 independent samples collected at 17 different scanning locations, all using 3 Tesla scanners. The hierarchical Bayesian approach uses partial pooling where site-specific parameters share a common prior distribution (Inverse Gamma(2,2) for site effects, Uniform(1,8) for GP length scale). Sample sizes varied slightly between models due to different missing value handling: ComBat accepts missing values (n=391 training, n=168 test for HC), while ComBat-GAM does not (n=370 training, n=156 test after excluding subjects with any missing values across 35 regions). The normative modeling was performed region-wise and independently for each of the 35 cortical measures (34 bilateral regions plus average). Supplementary materials contain extensive model diagnostics including convergence metrics (R̂ < 1.05 for all parameters), effective sample sizes, and trace plots for all four chains. The paper also reports detailed comparisons of effect sizes for site effects before and after correction, showing substantial reduction (partial η² from 0.55-0.58 in raw data to <0.001-0.17 after correction). Monte-Carlo sampling used 4000 iterations with 2000 warm-up iterations discarded. The study compared against five comparison models: ComBat, modified ComBat (preserving age/sex), ComBat-GAM, residuals (regressing out site), and raw data. All models except HBLM and HBGPM used a two-stage approach: first harmonize, then apply simple Bayesian linear model without site predictor.
